title: Discuss development, utilisation and management of human and natural resources

lessons.title: Natural resources on the farm
lessons.html:
Natural resources on the farm

Natural resources are things from nature that we use to farm and to live. A farm cannot work without them. The main natural resources on a farm are:

  • Soil: plants grow in it. Good topsoil takes hundreds of years to form but can wash away in one storm.
  • Water: from rivers, dams, boreholes and rain. Animals, crops and people all need it.
  • Veld and grazing: the grass and bushes that cattle, sheep and goats eat.
  • Plants and trees: for shade, firewood, wind breaks and food for wild animals.
  • Wild animals and insects: bees pollinate crops; birds eat insects.
  • Sun and air: plants need sunlight to grow.

Using resources wisely

Some resources run out or get damaged if we use them badly. Wise use means using them today in a way that still leaves enough for the future.

Bad useWise use
Too many cattle in one camp, so the veld becomes bareMove animals between camps and rest the veld
Ploughing up and down a slopePloughing across the slope (on the contour)
Leaving taps and troughs leakingFixing leaks quickly and watering at the right time
Throwing chemical containers in the riverReturning empty containers as the label says

The law protects resources

South Africa has laws to protect natural resources. The Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 deals with protecting soil, veld and water on farms and controlling weeds and invader plants. The National Water Act 36 of 1998 controls how water is used. Your farm manager must follow these laws, and you help by working carefully.

What you can do

  • Report erosion gullies, broken fences and leaking pipes.
  • Do not make fires in the veld.
  • Close gates so animals stay in the right camp.
  • Keep rubbish and chemicals out of rivers and dams.

lessons.title: People as a resource
lessons.html:
People as a resource

Human resources are the people who work on the farm: workers, supervisors, managers and the owner. People are the most important resource. Machines and land do nothing without people who know how to use them.

Developing people

Developing people means helping them learn and grow. A farm develops its people by:

  • giving training, like this course, on safety, animals, crops and machines;
  • showing new workers how a job is done and checking on them;
  • giving people more responsibility when they are ready, for example making a good worker a team leader;
  • supporting adult education so workers can read, write and count better.

When workers learn new skills, the farm does better work and the workers can earn more.

Using people well

Using people well means putting the right person on the right job. A worker who is good with animals may be best in the dairy. A worker who can drive and is careful may be trained on the tractor. Good planning also means not giving one person too much work while others stand around.

Managing people

Managers and supervisors manage people by:

  • explaining clearly what must be done, by when and how well;
  • treating everyone fairly and with respect;
  • following labour law on hours, leave and pay;
  • keeping workers safe, as the Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 requires;
  • listening to workers' ideas and problems.

Your part

Every worker is also responsible. Come to work on time, do the job properly, look after tools, ask when you do not understand and share what you know with others. Teamwork makes the whole farm stronger.

Key points

  • Natural resources include soil, water, veld, plants, animals, sun and air.
  • Wise use leaves enough resources for the future, for example resting veld and ploughing on the contour.
  • Laws such as Act 43 of 1983 and the National Water Act protect farm resources.
  • People are the most important farm resource.
  • Develop people through training, use them in the right jobs and manage them fairly and safely.
